planting.note: Plant a bare-root or grafted tree while still dormant in late winter, in deep, well-drained soil; Niitaka needs roughly 400-450 hours of winter chill and a different Asian pear cultivar such as Hosui or Shinseiki blooming nearby for pollination.

directions: Niitaka is a Japanese-bred nashi pear noted for producing some of the largest fruit of any commonly grown Asian pear cultivar, often exceeding a pound once thinned to one fruit per spur cluster. The round fruit carries a warm brown russeted skin over crisp, very juicy flesh with a mild, sweet flavor and none of the graininess of unripe European pears. Trees ripen fruit in September and, unlike European pears, the fruit should be picked when fully colored since it will not continue to ripen or improve once removed from the tree.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Asian Pear Varieties
University of California Cooperative Extension
California Rare Fruit Growers — Asian Pear Fact Sheet

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil; Akizuki blooms and ripens in the same general window as Nijisseiki and benefits from a different Asian pear cultivar planted nearby as a pollinator.

directions: Bred in Japan and released as a newer alternative to older russet cultivars, Akizuki produces large, round, brown-gold fruit with a flavor that is notably sweeter and lower in acid than many older Asian pear cultivars. The flesh is crisp and stays firm in storage longer than most nashi types, which has made it popular with growers who want an extended eating window after harvest. It ripens in mid-to-late season, generally after Hosui and Shinseiki but before Korean Giant, and requires cross-pollination to set a full crop.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Asian Pear Varieties
University of California Cooperative Extension
California Rare Fruit Growers — Asian Pear Fact Sheet

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in late winter while dormant in full sun and well-drained soil; Hakuho ripens earlier than most Japanese pear cultivars and needs another Asian pear variety nearby for pollination.

directions: Hakuho is an older mid-20th-century Japanese cultivar distinguished from Hosui and Niitaka by its smooth, pale yellow-green skin rather than a russeted brown finish. The large fruit is very juicy with mild, well-balanced sweetness and less of the aromatic intensity of newer cultivars, but it ripens earlier in the season, typically in late July to early August in warm climates. It has historically been used by Japanese breeders as parent stock for several later-introduced pear cultivars valued for earliness.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension
California Rare Fruit Growers — Asian Pear Fact Sheet
Washington State University Tree Fruit Research and Extension Center

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun; Kikusui is a lighter, less vigorous bearer than modern cultivars and benefits from a nearby Asian pear pollinator such as Hosui.

directions: Kikusui is an early-1900s Japanese heirloom whose name translates to 'chrysanthemum water,' a reference to the fruit's exceptionally high juice content when bitten into. The skin is smooth and pale green-yellow rather than russeted, and the mildly sweet, watery flesh has a softer texture than firmer modern nashi cultivars. It bears less heavily than newer selections bred for commercial production, which keeps it mostly in the hands of heirloom collectors and home orchardists rather than commercial growers today.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Asian Pear Fact Sheet
University of California Cooperative Extension
Oregon State University Extension — Asian Pear Varieties

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil; Tsu Li needs only around 150-200 hours of winter chill, making it one of the more dependable Asian pear cultivars for mild Gulf Coast winters, and it also serves as a useful pollinator for other low-chill Asian pears.

directions: Tsu Li is a Chinese heirloom pear grown widely across the Gulf South, valued for a chilling requirement low enough to fruit reliably where many other Asian pear cultivars fail to set a full crop in mild winters. The bottle-shaped fruit has smooth green-yellow skin and firmer, less crisp flesh than typical round nashi types, with a mild sweet flavor that leans closer to a European pear than to crunchy cultivars like Hosui. Trees show good field resistance to fire blight, a major disease pressure in the humid Southeast, and are commonly recommended alongside cultivars like Orient and Southern King for home orchards in Texas and Louisiana.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension
LSU AgCenter
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension

common_name: Nishimura Wase Persimmon (Early-Ripening Japanese Astringent Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Nishimura Wase is an astringent cultivar and, like Hachiya, must fully soften to a jelly-like consistency before eating.

directions: Nishimura Wase is a Japanese astringent persimmon whose main distinction from cultivars like Hachiya and Tanenashi is timing: it colors and ripens several weeks earlier in the season, extending the harvest window into late summer in warm climates. The medium-large, acorn-shaped fruit has deep orange-red skin and, like other astringent types, must be allowed to fully soften on the counter or after a hard freeze before the tannins mellow into a sweet, rich flavor. It is grown alongside later-ripening cultivars in California's Central Valley to spread out the persimmon harvest season.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Persimmon Fact Sheet
University of California Cooperative Extension
UC Davis Fruit & Nut Research & Information Center

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil; O'Gosho is self-fruitful and non-astringent, so fruit can be eaten firm as soon as it colors, without needing to soften first.

directions: O'Gosho is a non-astringent Japanese persimmon that stays notably more compact than standard Fuyu, making it a practical choice for smaller home orchards or espalier training. The fruit is smaller and rounder than Fuyu with a slightly flattened shape and orange-red skin, and it can be harvested and eaten crisp like an apple as soon as full color develops. Being self-fruitful, a single tree sets a complete crop without a separate pollinator variety nearby.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Persimmon Fact Sheet
University of California Cooperative Extension
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Persimmon Production

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in a hot, sunny site; Triumph is astringent and, for home eating, should be left to fully soften like Hachiya rather than eaten firm.

directions: Triumph is an astringent persimmon bred in Israel and marketed commercially worldwide under the trade name Sharon Fruit after a de-astringency treatment, though home gardeners can simply let the fruit ripen fully soft on the counter as with any other astringent cultivar. The medium, round, orange fruit is nearly seedless and develops a mild, honeyed flavor once fully ripe, without the pronounced tannins of firm fruit. It performs especially well in hot, dry summer climates and has become an important commercial cultivar in Israel, Spain, and California's Central Valley.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Persimmon Fact Sheet
University of California Cooperative Extension
UC Davis Fruit & Nut Research & Information Center

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Tsurunoko is astringent and needs to fully soften to a jelly-like texture before it is palatable, the same as Hachiya or Tanenashi.

directions: Tsurunoko is an old Japanese heirloom whose name translates to 'crane's egg,' describing the fruit's distinctive elongated shape with a pointed tip unlike the flatter or acorn-shaped fruit of most other persimmon cultivars. The deep orange skin covers flesh that becomes exceptionally sweet and jelly-soft once the astringency fully resolves after ripening. It remains a specialty planting favored by home orchardists and heirloom collectors rather than a mainstream commercial cultivar.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Persimmon Fact Sheet
University of California Cooperative Extension
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Persimmon Production
